title: Mirabai
hook: messengers arrive at Dwarka to bring Mira home, and she asks for one more visit to the temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai and the stamp at the end of her songs: Mira's Lord is Giridhar. Did you pass something on with a name attached? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

A delegation from home stands at the door. They've traveled a long way, to the far western coast, to a temple town by the sea. They've been sent to bring a woman back, and they aren't supposed to return without her. She listens. She doesn't say no. She asks for one thing first: let me go to the temple once more. The town is Dwarka, the city tradition gives to Krishna in his later life. The woman is Mira. And today, on our last day with her, the story tradition tells about how her road ended.
screen: `A DELEGATION AT THE DOOR.` → `DWARKA, BY THE SEA.` → `HOW HER ROAD ENDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in paraphrase, and it's tradition's story, not a record. After Vrindavan, Mira travels on to Dwarka, the city of Krishna as a king, where he is worshipped in the temple as Ranchhod, among other names. She sings there. Meanwhile, back in Mewar, things have gone badly, and some tellings say the royal house comes to believe its troubles began when Mira was driven out. So messengers are sent, some say priests among them, to bring her home. They plead. Some tellings say they threaten to fast until she agrees. Mira asks only to go into the temple first, to take leave of her Lord. She goes in, and she doesn't come out. Tradition says that she merged into the image of Krishna, and that her sari was found wrapped around it. Step back and look at the shape of her whole road in the songs and stories: the palace, the temple floor with bells on her feet, Vrindavan, Dwarka, and then into the shrine. Every step moves her closer to Krishna and further from what others had planned for her. Then set her beside another. Andal's story, a few days ago, ends almost the same way, with a woman going into a shrine and not coming out. Two women, two languages, far apart, and the tradition tells both their endings as union, not death. Last, notice what Mira doesn't do. She doesn't refuse the messengers to their faces, or run. She asks for one last visit. In the story, that's all she needs.
screen: `MESSENGERS SENT TO DWARKA` · `ONE LAST VISIT TO THE TEMPLE` · `HER SARI AROUND THE IMAGE` · `A ROAD THAT ENDS IN UNION`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one more visit. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a place that matters to you: a room, a temple, a kitchen, a stretch of shore. Picture going in once more, slowly, the way Mira asked to. Notice the light, the sounds, what's on the walls. Stay there a while. Nobody is hurrying you. If you pray, you can take leave of that place with a word of thanks. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai. Tradition says that at Dwarka, asked to come home, she went into the temple for one last visit, and only her sari was found, wrapped around Krishna's image. Today's word.
Your line: Mirabai. Today, before you leave somewhere you love, pause at the door for one more look. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to Krishna's temple at Dwarka hear the story of Mira's last visit, and devotees remember her with her songs at Dwarka, in Vrindavan and in Rajasthan.

original.note: Sanskrit: Dwarka, Krishna's city by the sea, where tradition says Mira's road ended.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mira's story ends when she dies, far from home.
what it means: tradition says she went into the temple at Dwarka and merged into Krishna's image, leaving only her sari.
what a scholar hears: the tradition tells her ending as union, the same shape it gives Andal's, and none of it comes from her own songs.

sources.ref: Hagiographical tradition of Mirabai: the messengers at Dwarka and her merging into the image

notes: The Dwarka ending is told as tradition. Confirm details: messengers (Brahmins) from Mewar, the threat to fast (dharna), Mira's request to take leave of Ranchhodji, and the sari found on the image. Tellings vary.
'Some tellings say the royal house comes to believe its troubles began when Mira was driven out': confirm this is a common element, or cut.
Ranchhod as a name of Krishna at Dwarka (Ranchhodrai/Dwarkadhish); confirm.
The comparison with Andal is within the same tradition (two Hindu women saints), not across religions; check tone.
Mewar and Dwarka are named without dates or distances.
Editor: Andal was last week (1353–1355; 1358 closed the week), so 'earlier this week' became 'a few days ago'; varied the 'turn it' transitions.
